turns.prompt_text: My friend who lives up in Boone has issues with squirrels. He is surrounded by cornfields and his property is plenty of trees and is very nice Because of this he is animal issues. The squirrels chewed through his Chevy Silverado wires and now he has problems with his truck We don't know for sure it was the squirrels but we have a good guess
turns.response_html:
That is an incredibly frustrating (and surprisingly common) problem. Boone’s mix of cornfields and large trees is basically a five-star resort for rodents, and unfortunately, modern vehicles are often collateral damage.

It is highly likely that squirrels (or mice) are the culprits. A major reason this happens is that many modern vehicle manufacturers, including Chevy, use soy-based insulation for their wiring harnesses to be more eco-friendly. To a hungry or nesting rodent, the wiring under the hood of that Silverado is essentially a warm, sheltered snack dispenser.

How to Confirm It's Squirrels

Before he starts repairing wires, he should pop the hood and look for the telltale signs of rodents:

  • The Pantry: Look for acorn shells, corn kernels from the nearby fields, or seed husks tucked into the crevices of the engine bay (especially near the battery tray or under the engine cover).
  • The Nest: Look for piled-up leaves, twigs, dried grass, or shredded hood-liner insulation.
  • The Damage: Rodent damage usually leaves wires looking frayed and gnawed at the ends, rather than cleanly sliced.

How to Stop It from Happening Again

Once he gets the wiring repaired (which he might want to run through his comprehensive auto insurance, as full harness replacements can be very expensive), he needs to make the truck an unwelcoming environment:

  1. Honda Rodent Tape: This is the gold standard among mechanics. Honda sells a specific electrical tape laced with capsaicin (the chemical that makes chili peppers hot). Wrapping the vulnerable wiring harnesses in this tape is a massive deterrent.
  2. Repellent Sprays: Sprays containing peppermint oil or bitter apple can be sprayed under the hood and around the wheel wells. The downside is that they wash off and need to be reapplied frequently.
  3. Light and Noise: Rodents want dark, quiet places to nest. Installing a battery-operated strobe light or ultrasonic rodent repeller under the hood can keep them away.
  4. Leave the Hood Up: If his truck is parked in a secure garage or pole barn, simply leaving the hood open overnight removes the "dark and sheltered" aspect that rodents look for when seeking a nesting spot.

turns.prompt_text: This makes me wonder if it's such a common problem then why hasn't it been solved yet?
turns.response_html:
It comes down to a stubborn mix of biology, economics, and legal technicalities. Here is why the automotive industry hasn't engineered this problem away:

The Biological Reality

Rodent incisors never stop growing, meaning they have to constantly gnaw on objects to file their teeth down. While soy might be more attractive to them as a snack, rodents were routinely chewing through petroleum-based wires, rubber hoses, and plastic reservoirs for decades before the industry switched materials. Because rodents are biologically driven to chew, reverting to older plastics wouldn't actually "solve" the problem.

Cost and Sustainability

Automakers are under intense pressure to use sustainable, biodegradable materials and reduce their reliance on petroleum. Soy-based plastics hit two massive targets for the industry: they are significantly more eco-friendly, and they are cheaper to manufacture at a global scale.

The Legal Precedent

Furious car owners have filed numerous class-action lawsuits against major manufacturers like Toyota, Honda, and Ford over the years, arguing that soy wiring is a design defect. However, the automakers keep winning. Federal courts have largely ruled that an animal destroying a car is an "environmental hazard" or an "act of nature," not a factory defect that falls under a manufacturer's warranty.

Zero Financial Incentive

Because the courts protect the manufacturers from warranty claims, the thousands of dollars in repair costs fall squarely on the vehicle owners and their auto insurance companies. Without massive warranty payouts threatening their bottom lines, automakers have no urgent financial reason to abandon a cheap, eco-friendly material in order to chase a "rodent-proof" wire that might not even be possible to create.

turns.prompt_text: Okay, so sounds like an unfortunate situation where no one's taking responsibility, but it sounds like it's a pretty easy solution as well. If it's just wires, I feel like that's something I could do myself
turns.response_html:
You can absolutely fix this yourself if you are comfortable working with basic hand tools. However, repairing modern automotive wiring requires a specific approach because the engine bay is a harsh environment full of heat, moisture, and extreme vibration.

While many people assume they should break out the soldering iron, the aerospace and automotive manufacturing industries actually advise against it. Solder creates a rigid joint in the wire; under constant engine vibration, that rigid joint can fatigue and crack. The OEM-approved repair method is actually crimping, but it has to be done correctly.

Here is exactly what you need and how to do it so the repair outlasts the truck.

The Right Tools for the Job

Do not use the cheap, hard plastic crimp connectors found in bargain bins—they do not seal out moisture and will eventually corrode. You want:

  1. Adhesive-Lined Heat Shrink Butt Connectors: These have a heat-activated glue inside. When you shrink them, the glue melts and creates a 100% waterproof, gas-tight seal around the wire.
  2. A Ratcheting Crimper: Standard plier-style crimpers rely on your grip strength, which often leads to under-crimped wires that pull out. A ratcheting crimper applies exact, uniform pressure and won't release until the perfect crimp is achieved.
  3. A Heat Gun: To activate the shrink tubing and melt the internal adhesive.

How to Make the Repair

If the squirrels chewed away a significant chunk of wire, you will need to splice in a new piece of wire (ensure it is the same gauge as the original).

Crucial Warning for Modern Trucks: Pay close attention to the wires you are fixing. If the squirrels chewed through a pair of wires that are tightly twisted around each other, those are CAN bus lines (the data network that allows the truck's computers to talk to each other). If you splice in new wire, you must maintain that exact twist rate (usually about one twist per inch) and keep the wire lengths identical. If they are left untwisted, electromagnetic interference can scramble the data and cause the truck to throw endless error codes.
